questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2t-9{t}^{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=-2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t-9{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=-2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =(1)^{2}-3(1)^{3}+C \\ -2 & =1-3+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=2\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =(2)^{2}-3(2)^{3} \\  & =4-24 \\  & =-20\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $20\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. Given that it is at rest when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration $a(t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t),$ where $a(t)$ is measured in ${\text{m/s}}^{2}$ and $t$ is measured in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{4}{5}\,\text{m/s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, calculate the speed of the particle at the moment $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4(-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t))+C \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=\frac{4}{5}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{5} & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot 0)+C \\ \frac{4}{5} & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+C \\ \frac{4}{5} & =\frac{4}{5}\cdot 1+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=\frac{\pi }{5}\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{\pi }{5}) & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\cdot \frac{\pi }{5}) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\cdot (-1) \\  & =-\frac{4}{5} \\  & =-0.8\,\text{m/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the speed is equal to $|v(t)|,$ we conclude that the speed of the particle is $0.8\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (14{t}^{6}+12{t}^{3})\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{7}+3{t}^{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=310.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}310 & =2({2}^{7})+3({2}^{4})+C \\ 310 & =304+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{7}+3{t}^{4}+6.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15{t}^{4}+6{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & =3{t}^{5}+2{t}^{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(2)=100.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}100 & =3({2}^{5})+2({2}^{3})+C \\ 100 & =96+16+C \\ 100 & =112+C \\ C & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{t}^{5}+2{t}^{3}-12.$
